# Agent briefing — Viktor Challenge: Build the Router

You are helping a hackathon team at TUM.ai (22–23 Aug 2026). The task: from an offline export
of real agent trajectories, build a **model router** and an **honest off-policy evaluation** of it.

## Guided workflows (read the one you need, follow it step by step)

- `skills/setup/SKILL.md` — environment + dataset setup, sanity checks, first baseline
- `skills/make-presentation/SKILL.md` — Viktor-branded presentation of the solution
- `skills/prepare-submission/SKILL.md` — package the solution into a formal submission

## The dataset (export of real Viktor trajectories)

The export ships as `trajectories_v1_<index>.jsonl.tar.gz` archives (links posted at
kickoff). Each extracts to one JSONL chunk:

```
export/
└─ trajectories_v1_*.jsonl   # one line = one real LLM request
```

Each JSONL line is one LLM request in the OpenAI-compatible Responses format, with exactly
three fields:

- `model` — the model id that served the call (~9 ids across two families and several
  generations): `claude-opus-5`, `claude-sonnet-5`, `claude-fable-5`, `claude-opus-4-8`,
  `gpt-5.6-sol`, `gpt-5.6-terra`, `gpt-5.6-luna`, ... These are real models with real
  prices — see the official schedule in `scripts/cost_model.py` (`fable-5` is the most
  expensive; `gpt-5.6-luna` the cheapest).
- `input` — full request history: `message` items (system/user/assistant; content parts are
  `input_text` and `input_image`), `function_call` / `function_call_output`,
  `custom_tool_call` / `custom_tool_call_output` (e.g. `apply_patch`), and `reasoning`
  items (empty summaries; gpt-family only). Each call's input contains every item of the
  call before it.
- `tools` — the function definitions available to the call (the real Viktor toolset)

**There is no `output` and no `usage`.** Also no trajectory ids, no timing, no quality labels.
Some entities appear as placeholders — `<PERSON_ROBERT>`, `<PROJECT_NAME>`, `<COMPANY_A>`,
ids as `<ID_13>` — consistent within a trajectory, so references still resolve. Images are
placeholder data URLs (`[base64 image redacted]`).

Key consequences:
- **Trajectories must be reconstructed**: group requests by their opening messages (same
  system + first user text), order by input length. `scripts/load_trajectories.py` does this.
- **Earlier outputs are recoverable**: what the model returned on call *i* appears inside call
  *i+1*'s input (the `function_call` / assistant items). Only the final call's output is truly gone.
- **All token counts are estimates** (chars/4 in this repo — or bring a tokenizer). Say so in
  the writeup; never present estimated tokens as measured.
- **The cache trap:** providers cache the shared input prefix across a task's calls; a model
  switch resets that cache — calls after a switch pay full price for the whole prefix. With no
  `usage.cached_tokens`, the cached share is *inferred* from item-level prefix overlap.
  `scripts/cost_model.py` implements this.
- **One model serves all calls of a trajectory** (premise); the model varies across
  trajectories — that variation is the natural experiment. The loader flags violations.
- **Pricing is official**: the per-model schedule ships in `scripts/cost_model.py`
  (`scripts/pricing.json` overrides it if the organizers post updates). Output cost still
  can't be computed — the export has no outputs — so quote input-side numbers as such.

## The twist (off-policy evaluation)

The log shows only the model that actually ran. Estimating what a different route would have
cost/kept is the depth of the challenge: matching or weighting across trajectories, judge-model
rescoring of single calls. Name where the estimate can fail — that is scored, not penalized.

## Judging (3 criteria, weights announced at kickoff)

1. **Routing insight** — real, nameable structure in the traces beats a black box
2. **Evaluation rigor** — honest off-policy estimate, cache-aware pricing
3. **Presentation clarity** — 5 minutes: one chart, one claim, one known weakness

Special prize: best off-policy-evaluation insight. Headline artifact: the **cost–quality frontier**, not a single point.

## Hard rules for you, the agent

- Dataset is **challenge use only, no redistribution** — never upload it anywhere or commit it
  to git (`export/` is gitignored; keep it there).
- If the organizers post schema notes or a price sheet that contradicts this document, trust them.
- Don't invent rules, deadlines, prizes, or credits — the team should ask in the challenge Discord.
- Keep everything runnable offline on a laptop: no GPUs, no API keys required
  (judge-model rescoring with the team's own keys is allowed).
# Viktor Challenge Starter — Build the Router

Starter kit for the **Viktor Challenge** at the TUM.ai hackathon (Munich, 22–23 Aug 2026).
From real LLM-request logs, build a router that picks the right model for every call —
then prove it works, even though the log shows only the model that ran, and no outputs or token counts.

## Quick start (5 minutes)

```bash
# 1. No dataset yet? Generate a synthetic sample with the same shape:
python scripts/make_synthetic_sample.py            # writes ./export/

# 2. Got the real dataset links (shipped at kickoff)? Then instead: the export ships
#    as trajectories_v1_<index>.jsonl.tar.gz archives — download, verify the posted
#    SHA-256, then:  mkdir -p export && tar xzf trajectories_v1_01.jsonl.tar.gz -C export/

# 3. Sanity-check the export, reconstruct trajectories, print stats:
python scripts/load_trajectories.py export/

# 4. Run the baseline heuristic router + cache-aware cost report:
python scripts/baseline_router.py export/

# 5. Turn results into a cost–quality frontier CSV (+ PNG if matplotlib is installed):
python scripts/plot_frontier.py results/routes.jsonl
```

Python 3.10+, standard library only (matplotlib optional for the PNG).

## Routemaxxing

The challenge implementation corrects the unit of analysis before routing: the real
chunk's 1,000 unique rows unfold into 10,845 model turns. It trains an interpretable,
family-preserving downgrade policy and reports a public-validation frontier with a
2-percentage-point proxy-quality constraint:

```bash
python scripts/routemaxxing.py export/
```

The command writes the certified and one-escalation route ledgers, frontier CSV/SVG,
and a fully traceable summary under `results/routemaxxing/`. It also writes
`results/routemaxxing.jsonl` for the local explorer and refreshes
`presentation-routemaxxing.html`. All token and dollar figures are estimates; final
outputs are excluded in the briefing-compatible primary analysis, and adaptive quality
is explicitly conditional on the logged context.

### Live demo

The aggregate-only Router Lab is deployable as a static GitHub Pages site:

```bash
python scripts/build_live_demo.py
python -m http.server 4173 -d docs
```

Open <http://127.0.0.1:4173>. The live deployment is
<https://utkukalkanli.github.io/routemaxxing/>. The page contains the interactive
certified policy, a cache-aware cost simulator, the validation frontier, and required
comparisons. It deliberately ships no challenge trajectories, prompts, tools, or route
ids. `.github/workflows/pages.yml` can deploy `docs/` from this repository after its
owner enables GitHub Pages with GitHub Actions as the source.

## Using a coding agent

Point Claude Code / Codex / Cursor / opencode at this repo — `AGENTS.md` briefs your agent.
In Claude Code you also get slash commands:

- `/setup` — set up everything needed to participate
- `/make-presentation` — build a Viktor-branded presentation of your solution
- `/prepare-submission` — package your solution into a formal submission

# Routemaxxing

Routemaxxing minimizes estimated, cache-aware model cost subject to a two-percentage-
point upper bound on automatic failure-proxy degradation. It runs fully offline and
uses only information available before each routing decision.

## The structural finding

The public chunk contains 1,000 unique histories. Their item sequences unfold into
10,845 model turns: model-authored runs produce tool calls or prose, and environment
items close one call and begin the next. The briefing-compatible analysis treats the
last output of every trajectory as unobservable.

The two model families also have disjoint tool dialects. Claude histories expose
`bash`/`file_edit`; GPT histories expose `shell_command`/`apply_patch`. Routemaxxing
therefore routes only within a family rather than inventing an unsupported cross-family
counterfactual.

## Policy

The certified policy reads only call-zero information: the opening task, trigger,
toolset, initial size, images, and nameable intent flags. It generates only strictly
cheaper, propensity-supported downgrades within the tool-dialect family. Proposals must
save money under both fixed-shape and behavior-adjusted cost, are ranked by training-only
partially pooled dollars saved per unit of predicted proxy-failure risk, and are admitted
by a threshold selected on training data. The savings predictor sees opening intent,
initial size, trigger, image, and surface—not realized depth or future outputs. The
selected model is kept for the whole trajectory.

The winning public policy admits every positive-savings supported proposal. This is not
an unbounded extrapolation: the full-adoption point won the training-only sweep while
its routed effective sample size stayed above 15 and its one-sided proxy-failure upper
bound stayed below +2 points. Unsupported defaults fall back unchanged. In particular,
GPT Luna has only 12 training trajectories versus the fixed minimum of 20, so the
certified router never selects it.

The adaptive policy starts from the certified choice and may escalate once after an
observed tool error, repeated action, or high-risk context growth. It never downgrades
or exceeds the original default, and it switches only if savings banked so far pay for
the full cache reset at that call. Its result is explicitly conditional on logged
states: a different early model could have generated a different later context.

## Evaluation

- Deterministic 70/30 split grouped by recoverable thread identity, falling back to the
  stable trajectory hash.
- L2 logistic outcome models and multinomial propensity models trained on the public
  training split. Enriched opening features and partial propensity pooling are reported
  as ablations; neither unlocked more routes than the simpler v1 feature model.
- Downgrade-from-default effects estimated with propensity-screened outcome regression;
  unsupported actions fall back to the configured model.
- Two thousand trajectory bootstrap replicates provide the one-sided 95% upper bound.
- Cost includes estimated uncached input, cached prefix reads, and every observable
  output. A switch resets the accumulated cache. Tokens are serialized JSON chars/4,
  never measured usage.
- Primary proxy evaluation excludes terminal assistant language because each
  trajectory's final output is unobservable under the challenge premise. A separately
  named sensitivity adds that language back.
- Behavior-adjusted cost uses training-only, partially pooled model × opening-intent ×
  initial-size estimates for observable output length. Fixed-shape cost is reported
  alongside it.

The primary automatic failure proxy combines an unresolved observable tool error and
repeated identical-action loops. It is not measured task quality. The terminal-language
sensitivity is also a proxy, not a label.
The organizer-held-out split is not present yet, so public-validation numbers must not
be presented as final held-out results.

## Reproduce

```bash
python scripts/routemaxxing.py export/
python -m pytest -q
python -m explorer
```

Generated evidence is under `results/routemaxxing/`. `ablation_comparison.csv` contains
the logged, heuristic, current, ablation, final, and conditional-adaptive rows;
`training_sweep.csv` records every training-only knob; `proposal_rankings.csv` exposes
the dollar/risk ordering; and `propensity_support.json` documents Luna's exclusion. The
model- and context-specific observable-output estimates are in
`output_length_sensitivity.json`. The explorer-compatible route is
`results/routemaxxing.jsonl`; the six-slide deck is
`presentation-routemaxxing.html`.
----
# Contextual cost router

The implementation is in `scripts/routers/v2_oracle.py`. It is additive: none of the
starter scripts are changed.

## Run

```bash
python3.13 scripts/routers/v2_oracle.py export/
```

This writes versioned routes plus `results/oracle_router/comparison.csv`,
`grouped_validation.csv`, `sensitivity.csv`, `frontier.csv`, `calibration.json`,
and `REPORT.md`.

For online use, fit once on historical rows and call the router on the first request:

```python
from scripts.routers.v2_oracle import fit_router

router = fit_router(historical_complete_rows, version="router_v4_conservative")
decision = router.route(first_request)
model = decision["model"]
per_model_estimates = decision["estimates"]
```

Each candidate estimate contains conditional-mean future uncached input, cached input,
output tokens, official-price spend, a separate typical-length `total_tokens_p50`, the
execution-quality proxy, uncertainty, and matched support. The online feature extractor
stops before the first model-produced item.

## Important correction to the starter assumption

In the supplied real chunk, each of the 1,000 JSONL rows is a complete trajectory.
Model-produced runs inside the row reconstruct 10,845 billed calls. Grouping rows by
opening text incorrectly produces 953 groups, including 19 mixed-model collisions.

Call decomposition recovers roughly 2.62M estimated output tokens. On the corrected,
cache-aware input+output ledger, logged spend is $278.36; treating each row as one
input-only request materially undercounts it. Every token number is still a chars/4
estimate because provider usage is absent.

## Versions

| Version | Idea | Estimated spend | Saving vs logged | Outcome proxy |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Corrected starter | Final-size `<15k` switch; future-leaking reference | $265.85 | 4.5% | 0.9891 |
| v2 workload | Predict workload; cheap below median, capable default above | $246.26 | 11.5% | 0.9909 |
| v3 matched | Cheapest matched model within 0.8 proxy points of best | $184.75 | 33.6% | 0.9861 |
| v4 conservative | Quality tolerance + uncertainty + 95% support radius | $138.00 | 50.4% | 0.9890 |
| v5 near-oracle | Aggressive same-family cost optimum | $120.48 | 56.7% | 0.9890 |
| v6 analogue | v4 plus aggressive routing for recurring task templates | $136.77 | 50.9% | 0.9879 |
| Same-trace floor | Cheapest same-family rate on realized quantities | $100.85 | 63.8% | unknowable |

v5 captures about 89% of the gap from logged spend to the same-trace cost floor, but
its GPT decision rests on only 20 logged Luna trajectories. v4 is the recommended
defensible policy and is 48.1% cheaper than the corrected starter. Its paired quality
difference from logged is +0.0004 with a 95% bootstrap interval of
[-0.0041, +0.0048]: no detected change, not proof of equivalence.

## Evaluation

- Five-fold cross-fitting: a trajectory is never used to predict itself.
- A second task-grouped five-fold check prevents recurring templates crossing folds.
- Transparent lexical/structural nearest-neighbour matching.
- Training-only recurring-task analogue calibration.
- Local behavior propensities and a 0.05-clipped doubly robust estimator.
- Propensity-floor sensitivity from 0.02 through 0.20 ($138.00–$139.12 for v4).
- Whole-trajectory, same-harness-family routing; no mid-task cache reset.
- High-precision tool failure/recovery proxy instead of the placeholder “kept model.”
- Paired bootstrap intervals for policy-minus-logged cost and quality.

Factual-action aggregate calibration is 0.908x actual cost and 0.880x actual expected
tokens. Expected cost/length remains heavy-tailed (cost MdAPE 64.4%, expected-token
MdAPE 98.2%). The separate p50 token forecast has 49.6% MdAPE overall and 28.0% for
known recurring templates. These are routing estimates, not precise invoices.

## Known limitations

Model assignment is observational, GPT/Claude harnesses have no useful cross-family
overlap, counterfactual models can change the trajectory itself, and the quality target
is an execution-completion proxy rather than a human label. The next export chunk must
be treated as untouched validation; selecting another frontier point on it would turn
it into training data.

# Routemaxxing **Spend the expensive model only where it matters.** A cost-aware LLM router for agent trajectories, with an honest off-policy evaluation: cache-aware pricing, propensity-supported downgrades, and an explicit proxy-risk bound. [![Live demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/live_demo-routemaxxing.vercel.app-6a4bff?style=for-the-badge&logo=vercel&logoColor=white)](https://routemaxxing.vercel.app)   [![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/python-3.10+-150079?style=for-the-badge&logo=python&logoColor=white)](#reproduce)   [![Hackathon](https://img.shields.io/badge/TUM.ai_×_Viktor-hackathon_2026-ff8a65?style=for-the-badge)](#context)
--- ## Result On a public validation split, the router cut estimated model spend by **45.8%** with no detected rise in the failure proxy: | | Estimated cost | Savings | Failure proxy Δ (upper 95%) | Routed coverage | |---|---:|---:|---:|---:| | Logged behavior | $88.88 | — | — | — | | Prompt-size heuristic baseline | $74.68 | 16.0% | −0.01 pp | 29.5% | | **Routemaxxing, certified** | **$48.18** | **45.8%** | **−0.19 pp** | **58.3%** | The constraint was an upper bound of +2 percentage points on failure-proxy degradation. The selected policy stays well inside it: its one-sided 95% upper bound is *negative*. It also leaves no supported expensive default unrouted.

> **Honesty notes.** Tokens are estimated (serialized JSON chars / 4), not measured. > The quality signal is an automatic failure proxy, not a human label. The numbers come > from the public validation split, not an organizer-held-out set. ## The problem You get an offline export of real agent trajectories (1,000 histories from a production agent across ~9 Claude and GPT models). The export has **no outputs, no token usage, and no quality labels**, and every trajectory shows only the model that actually ran. Two questions follow. Which model should each task get? And how do you *prove* a different choice would have been cheaper without being worse, when you never observe that choice? ## What we found 1. **The unit of analysis was wrong.** The 1,000 rows are not single requests. Each unfolds into a full history, and together they hold **10,845 model calls**. Grouping rows by opening text (the starter assumption) gives 953 groups, 19 of them mixed-model collisions, and badly undercounts spend. 2. **The two model families speak different tool dialects.** Claude histories use `bash`/`file_edit`; GPT histories use `shell_command`/`apply_patch`. They do not overlap, so a cross-family counterfactual has no support. The router only downgrades *within* a family. 3. **Switching models mid-task is expensive.** A provider's prompt cache is lost on every switch, so the next call pays full price for the whole prefix. The router picks one model per trajectory and prices that cache reset explicitly. ## How it works - **Decides at call zero.** The policy sees only the opening task, trigger, toolset, initial context size, images, and named intent flags. It never sees future depth, errors, or outputs. - **Proposes only supported downgrades.** It considers only strictly cheaper models within the same family that the logged data actually supports (minimum propensity and sample size). GPT Luna had 12 training trajectories, below the minimum of 20, so the certified router never picks it. - **Ranks proposals by dollars saved per unit of risk.** Uses partially pooled savings estimates and an L2 logistic failure model trained only on the training split. - **Evaluates off-policy.** Uses a 70/30 split grouped by thread identity, propensity-screened outcome regression, and 2,000 trajectory bootstrap replicates for the one-sided 95% bound. - **Prices with caching.** Cost includes uncached input, cached prefix reads, and every observable output, and a switch resets the cache. Fixed-shape and behavior-adjusted costs are both reported. - **Reports an adaptive variant separately.** A one-shot escalation policy runs only after observed tool errors or loops. Its result is conditional on the logged states, so it is kept out of the headline. Full write-ups: [`ROUTEMAXXING.md`](ROUTEMAXXING.md) (certified policy and evaluation) and [`ROUTER.md`](ROUTER.md) (earlier contextual-cost router, v2–v6). ## Known limitations - Model assignment is observational. A different early model could have produced a different later context. - The failure proxy covers unresolved tool errors and repeated-action loops. It does not measure task quality. - No cross-family routing, because the data has no overlap to support it. - All dollar figures are estimates from estimated tokens and the official price schedule. ## Reproduce Python 3.10+ with the standard library only. The challenge dataset is not redistributable, so it is not in this repo. A synthetic sample with the same shape is included: ```bash python scripts/make_synthetic_sample.py # writes ./export/ (or extract the real export there) python scripts/routemaxxing.py export/ # ledgers, frontier, summary → results/routemaxxing/ python -m pytest -q ``` Interactive tools: ```bash python scripts/build_live_demo.py # aggregate-only data → docs/data.js python -m http.server 4173 -d docs # Router Lab at http://127.0.0.1:4173 python -m explorer # local trajectory explorer (needs the export) ``` The live demo ships only aggregate metrics: no prompts, tools, trajectories, or route ids. ## Repository map | Path | What | |---|---| | `scripts/routemaxxing.py` | Certified router, off-policy evaluation, frontier | | `scripts/routers/` | Earlier router versions (heuristic, learned, contextual-oracle) | | `scripts/cost_model.py` | Cache-aware cost model and official price schedule | | `scripts/load_trajectories.py` | Export loader and trajectory reconstruction | | `docs/` | Static Router Lab, deployed to Vercel | | `explorer/` | Local trajectory explorer (Python API and frontend) | | `presentation-routemaxxing.html` | Six-slide hackathon deck ([PDF](presentation-routemaxxing.pdf)) | | `tests/` | Pytest suite | ## Context Built at the **TUM.ai hackathon** in Munich (22–23 Aug 2026) for the **Viktor Challenge: Build the Router**.
